content: Governments around the world sounded the alarm on Wednesday over a critical flaw in Java, one of the most widely used programming languages on the planet, warning that it could let hackers break into computer systems and take control of servers. The vulnerability, nicknamed Java4Shell and tracked as CVE-2026-114938, is the latest high-profile cyber incident in a month already marked by major software flaws and outages. Authorities in the United States, South Korea, Germany and Britain, along with China's Tencent, urged companies and organisations to install a fix immediately, while the Dutch cybersecurity agency said it was investigating the issue. The United States Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) said in an advisory that the vulnerability required immediate patching. The flaw was discovered by the US security firm Calif, which last month found a similar bug in another programming language, PHP, according to [a report by Reuters](https://www.gmanetwork.com/news/scitech/technology/1009998/java-flaw-leaves-systems-open-to-hackers-say-us-south-korea-china-s-tencent/story/). Calif said on Wednesday that it had found the bug in Java's memory functions, and Oracle, which maintains Java, issued a software update for its Java Development Kit on November 17 that contains the fix. The vulnerability is a heap overflow in the part of Java that decodes Base64, a common format applications use to send data such as login details and file uploads. According to Calif, a malformed Base64 string ending in bad padding can make the decoder write 62 or 63 bytes past the end of a heap buffer, corrupting the memory of the Java Virtual Machine. Calif says it chained that memory corruption into full remote code execution, meaning an attacker could run their own code on a server without logging in. The firm demonstrated the attack against default installations of several widely deployed products, including Atlassian Jira and Confluence, Jenkins, Keycloak, JFrog Artifactory and PingFederate. Oracle scores the flaw 8.1 out of 10 under the CVSS 3.1 system, rating it high severity, while Calif rates it 9.2 under CVSS 4.0, which puts it in the critical range. Red Hat, another major distributor, rates its impact as critical. The good news is that the flaw is not as universal as its nickname suggests. It lives only in a hardware-accelerated version of the Base64 decoder that runs on x86-64 processors with a feature called AVX-512 VBMI, found in newer Intel Xeon server chips from the Ice Lake generation onward and in AMD processors from the Zen 4 generation onward. The same Java build running on an older server, or on an ARM-based machine, is not affected. Affected versions are unpatched OpenJDK 17 builds from 17.0.6 onward, along with the Java 21, 25 and 27 release lines, across distributions including Amazon Corretto, Eclipse Temurin, Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, Azul Zulu, Red Hat OpenJDK and Oracle Java SE. Standard Java 8 and Java 11 installations do not contain the vulnerable decoder and need no patch for this flaw, although Oracle lists one exception, its Java SE 8 Enterprise Performance Pack build 8u511b33-perf. Fixed builds shipped on November 17: Oracle's Java SE releases 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1 and 27.0.1.1, with Amazon Corretto and Azul Zulu also releasing fixes the same day. Some distributors, including Temurin, Red Hat and Ubuntu, were still preparing their builds as of November 18, according to security researchers. For systems that cannot be updated right away, starting the Java Virtual Machine with the flag -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics disables the vulnerable code path as a temporary workaround. Concern was particularly acute in South Korea, where Java is heavily used across government and industry. The presidential office held an emergency meeting on Tuesday with government agencies to discuss preemptive measures, according to the Yonhap news agency, and South Korea's Ministry of Science and ICT and the Korea Internet and Security Agency said on Wednesday that public institutions and private enterprises must urgently install the security updates. Tencent Cloud, the cloud-computing arm of the Chinese technology company Tencent, warned customers that the flaw could allow unauthenticated attackers to steal sensitive information or take control of affected servers. As of November 18, no successful attacks exploiting the vulnerability had been publicly reported, according to German and Dutch cybersecurity agencies, and the flaw had not been added to CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue. Calif has published a proof of concept that triggers the bug without taking control of a system, but says it is withholding the exploit chains for individual applications for now. The timing has fed public anxiety. The warning comes days after a wave of technology outages in the United States, including a nationwide ground stop on November 13, and CISA was careful to say it had not linked the Java flaw to any recent outages. Security researchers say the episode echoes the Log4Shell crisis of December 2021, when a flaw in a Java logging library forced emergency patching across the world, though Java4Shell's reach is narrower because of the processor requirement. Calif's discovery also follows its PHP2Shell finding last month, which prompted emergency patches for the PHP programming language, underlining how flaws in the shared building blocks of the internet can put thousands of systems at risk at once. The practical advice from security agencies is straightforward: find out which Java version your servers run, check whether the processor supports AVX-512 VBMI, and install the November 17 update. Java is used in critical information systems spanning government agencies, banks, hospitals and the military, so even a flaw that needs a specific chip to bite is being treated as a race against the clock. The next few days will show whether attackers move faster than the patching. The warning lands in a month already full of technology alarms: [Google said artificial intelligence had carried out its first fully autonomous cyberattack](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/google-first-fully-autonomous-ai-cyberattack-november-2026), and [Apple blamed an internal update after iCloud, the App Store and Apple Pay went down](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/apple-services-outage-icloud-app-store-apple-pay-november-2026).
summary: Governments around the world have urged companies to patch a critical flaw in Java, dubbed Java4Shell, that could let attackers run code on servers without logging in. The bug, tracked as CVE-2026-114938, sits in the code that decodes Base64 data inside one of the world's most widely used programming languages.
title: Governments sound the alarm over 'Java4Shell' flaw that could let hackers take over servers
